item.title: Rajuk faces scrutiny over new sewage rules
item.description:
The government’s latest directive requiring buildings in Gulshan, Banani, Baridhara, and Niketan to install septic tanks, soak wells, and, in some cases, sewage treatment plants (STPs) has sparked debate over whether authorities are tackling environmental pollution or shifting the cost of years of planning and regulatory shortcomings onto property owners.
While Rajuk says the move is essential to stop untreated wastewater from polluting Gulshan Lake and groundwater, urban planners argue the directive has exposed deeper weaknesses in Dhaka’s building regulation, sewerage planning, and enforcement systems.
Under Bangladesh’s planning framework, Rajuk is responsible for approving building designs, ensuring compliance with construction rules, and verifying buildings before occupancy.
Experts question how thousands of buildings were approved if the wastewater management systems now being required were already mandatory under existing regulations.
“If mandatory sanitation facilities were absent, how were occupancy certificates issued in the first place?” asked one urban planning expert, arguing that regulatory failures cannot now be shifted entirely onto citizens.
Many property owners say they constructed their buildings according to Rajuk-approved designs, obtained legal utility connections, and have paid sewerage charges to Dhaka WASA for years.
They are now being instructed to retrofit expensive sanitation systems that may require significant structural modifications.
“We fully support protecting Gulshan Lake,” said a property owner in Gulshan, requesting anonymity.
“But if the authorities approved these buildings, connected them to the sewerage system, and collected sewerage fees for years, why are we now being told our sanitation systems are inadequate?”
The controversy has also revived questions about Bangladesh’s unfinished sewerage infrastructure.
The Tk3,482-crore Dasherkandi Sewage Treatment Plant, inaugurated in 2023, was expected to form the backbone of Dhaka’s modern wastewater management system. However, much of the capital remains outside the central sewerage network, leaving many neighborhoods dependent on decentralized wastewater disposal.
Urban planners question whether requiring costly building-level STPs before completing the city’s sewerage network reflects a coherent long-term strategy.
“Decentralized mandates without completing central sewerage reflect fragmented urban governance and shift responsibility to citizens,” said Adil Mohammed Khan, executive director of the Institute for Planning and Development (IPD) and a professor in the Department of Urban and Regional Planning at Jahangirnagar University.
Architect and urban development expert Iqbal Habib echoed those concerns, saying Dhaka’s sanitation crisis cannot be solved “building by building” but instead requires integrated citywide infrastructure planning backed by institutional accountability.
Urban governance specialists say sewerage systems, like roads and drainage, are core public infrastructure.
They argue that if the state has yet to complete the necessary network, requiring individual property owners to bear the full financial burden raises important policy questions.
Several experts recommend phased implementation, government incentives, technical assistance, and cost-sharing mechanisms rather than blanket compliance orders.
Rajuk, however, maintains that immediate intervention is necessary.
Chief Town Planner Mohammad Ashraful Islam said the 2025 Building Construction Rules require STPs in areas lacking effective sewerage coverage, while septic tanks and soak wells remain mandatory under the rules, even in areas served by sewer lines.
According to Rajuk, Dhaka’s existing sewerage coverage remains insufficient to rely solely on centralized treatment, making decentralized systems essential until the network is fully developed.
Environmental experts caution that residential buildings are only one of several sources of pollution entering Gulshan Lake.
Wastewater from commercial establishments, informal settlements, illegal sewer connections, stormwater drains, and aging infrastructure also contributes significantly to deteriorating water quality.
Previous surveys have identified numerous drainage outlets discharging untreated wastewater into the lake, suggesting the pollution originates from multiple sources rather than households alone.
Experts therefore call for comprehensive pollution mapping, independent technical audits of existing buildings, faster expansion of the central sewerage network, accelerated connections to the Dasherkandi treatment plant, and transparent enforcement based on scientific evidence.
Beyond septic tanks and STPs, they say the controversy raises broader questions about urban governance, regulatory accountability, and the state’s responsibility to provide essential public infrastructure.
While protecting Gulshan Lake is widely recognized as an environmental necessity, experts say long-term restoration will require more than stricter compliance.
It will also depend on coordinated investment, institutional accountability, and a clear, evidence-based strategy for expanding Dhaka’s sewerage infrastructure.

item.title: Why Fiji’s HIV surge matters for Bangladesh
item.description:
Thousands of Bangladeshi workers in Fiji and the country’s rapidly expanding HIV epidemic have prompted global health experts to urge Bangladesh and other Asian nations to strengthen harm reduction and HIV prevention before similar outbreaks take hold.
Speaking at the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026), experts pointed to Fiji’s experience as a warning of how quickly HIV can spread when infections among people who inject drugs are not brought under control.
The Pacific island nation, which now employs between 3,000 and 3,500 Bangladeshi workers, has recorded a 14-fold increase in new HIV diagnoses over the past five years.
The outbreak became so severe that Fiji declared a national HIV outbreak in January 2025 after infections spread from people who inject drugs into the wider population.
Responding to a question from Dhaka Tribune, Dr Jason Mitchell, chair of Fiji’s National HIV Outbreak Cluster Response Taskforce, said health authorities are monitoring HIV infections among migrant workers, although nationality-specific data are not available.
Experts said Fiji’s experience carries an important lesson for Bangladesh, where HIV prevalence remains low but continued investment in harm reduction is essential to prevent future outbreaks.
Md Akhtaruzzaman, senior manager for Management and Coordination at the AIDS/STD Program under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), said Bangladesh’s situation differs significantly because most yaba and methamphetamine users consume the drugs orally rather than by injection.
He said Bangladesh has an estimated 34,000 people who inject drugs, about 87% of whom are covered by harm reduction services, including needle and syringe exchange programs and methadone maintenance treatment.
“Our HIV program places strong emphasis on people who inject drugs through targeted harm reduction interventions,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Sustaining these services is essential for preventing HIV, sexually transmitted infections and hepatitis C.”
According to UNAIDS data presented at the conference, Fiji’s adult HIV prevalence has reached 1.2%, while the number of people living with HIV has risen from about 8,900 in 2025 to an estimated 12,000 this year.
Nearly two-thirds of new infections are among people aged 20 to 34.
The country’s treatment response has also fallen well short of global targets, with only about 40% of people living with HIV aware of their status, 22% receiving treatment and just 3.2% achieving viral suppression.
Dr Mitchell said the absence of a nationwide needle and syringe program remains one of the biggest gaps in Fiji’s response, allowing HIV transmission among people who inject drugs to continue.
Experts at AIDS 2026 said Fiji’s outbreak illustrates how rapidly HIV can spread beyond key populations if prevention, testing and treatment fail to keep pace with changing patterns of drug use.
They warned that maintaining evidence-based harm reduction programs is far less costly than responding to a rapidly expanding epidemic after it has spread into the general population.

item.title: Inside Salahuddin Ammar’s rise at Rajshahi University
item.description:
From forcing deans to resign and confronting university authorities to repeated allegations of violence, intimidation and administrative interference, Rucsu General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar has remained at the centre of one controversy after another.
A fresh attempted murder case has now raised broader questions over whether repeated institutional inaction emboldened one of the country’s most controversial student leaders.
For nearly a year, Rajshahi University has witnessed a steady stream of controversies surrounding Rajshahi University Central Students’ Union (Rucsu) General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar.
Each incident sparked criticism, protests or investigation committees. Yet none resulted in visible disciplinary action.
That pattern has now come under renewed scrutiny after a court directed the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) to investigate an attempted murder case against Ammar, Rucsu Assistant General Secretary SM Salman Sabbir and seven other student leaders over the alleged assault on student Mahmudul Hasan inside the university’s central library.
The case also names 17 to 18 unidentified people as accused.
The criminal case is the most serious legal challenge Ammar has faced since emerging as one of the most influential student leaders on campus.
But for many teachers and students, it is only the latest chapter in a series of incidents that they say gradually transformed him from an elected student representative into a figure capable of influencing administrative decisions and creating a climate of fear across the university.
According to the case filed by Mahmudul’s father, the victim was repeatedly assaulted with iron rods and bamboo sticks, dragged from an ambulance while being taken for treatment and beaten again.
The complaint further alleges that when the family first approached Motihar Police Station, police declined to accept the case, prompting them to seek relief through the court, which later referred the matter to the PBI for investigation.
Long before the latest case, Ammar had repeatedly drawn headlines.
During protests over the reinstatement of the “dependent quota” before the Rucsu election, he led demonstrations in which the then vice-chancellor’s vehicle was surrounded and university officials were confined inside an administrative building for hours.
The incident triggered widespread criticism, although Ammar denied physically assaulting any teacher.
After becoming Rucsu general secretary, allegations against him shifted from street protests to university administration.
Teachers accused him of interfering in administrative affairs, threatening faculty members and publicly pressuring deans to resign.
During one protest, resignation letters were displayed before journalists while administrative offices, including those of the vice-chancellor, registrar and proctor, were locked.
The university later relieved several deans of their duties following the standoff.
His activities also extended beyond campus administration.
A fundraising campaign seeking Tk76 lakh for a July anniversary concert drew criticism over transparency.
An eight-hour railway blockade over an unrelated student incident disrupted train services across the western region and, according to railway authorities, caused losses of around Tk35 lakh.
Controversial social media comments and political disputes further fuelled public debate.
Critics also repeatedly linked Ammar to earlier incidents of violence, including allegations over the death of a former Chhatra League leader in 2024.
Those allegations have been publicly denied by Ammar, and no conviction has been reported.
Despite the succession of controversies, university authorities acknowledge that while several investigation committees were formed over different incidents, their findings never resulted in publicly known disciplinary measures.
Teachers and student organisations argue that this lack of visible accountability allowed tensions to escalate over time.
The latest library assault has intensified those concerns.
The Democratic Student Alliance described the incident as “mob violence” and demanded a fair investigation.
Leaders of the Student Rights Council, Samajtantrik Chhatra Front and Chhatra Dal also called for those responsible to be punished, warning that repeated incidents were undermining the university’s academic environment and damaging its reputation nationwide.
Ammar has rejected the allegations, saying all of his actions were intended to protect students’ interests.
He claimed the library violence was a reaction to an attack on the Rucsu building by Chhatra League activists.
Rajshahi University Chhatra Shibir also denied responsibility for his actions, saying he is not a member of the organisation.
University authorities say the latest incident, along with earlier allegations, is now under investigation and that action will be taken once inquiry reports are submitted.
For many on campus, however, the central question is no longer about a single incident, but how repeated controversies were allowed to accumulate until they culminated in a criminal investigation.

item.title: DU suspends 3 teachers, relieves four others of key duties
item.description:
Three teachers of the University of Dhaka have been temporarily suspended, while four others have been relieved of all academic and administrative responsibilities over separate allegations of misconduct and irregularities.
The university’s Public Relations Office confirmed the decisions in a statement issued on Thursday, following a syndicate meeting held on July 28.
The meeting was chaired by Dhaka University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr ABM Obaidul Islam.
The suspended teachers are Professor Dr Sadeka Halim of the Department of Sociology, Professor Dr Md Shafiqul Islam of the Department of Nuclear Engineering, and Professor Dr Afroza Shelly.
Professor Sadeka Halim was suspended over allegations of unprofessional conduct inside and outside the classroom, ethical misconduct and other related issues. The other two teachers were suspended based on complaints from students of different batches and based on the findings of an inquiry committee.
The syndicate also removed Professor Dr Md Abdul Muhit of the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology from the post of department chairman and barred him from all academic and administrative duties over allegations of activities against the spirit of the July mass uprising, spreading propaganda against the university administration and the government, supporting a banned organisation, and issuing threats.
Prof Dr Abu Shara Shamsur Rouf of the Department of Pharmaceutical Technology and Prof Dr Rafiqul Islam (Rafiq Shahariar) of the Department of Peace and Conflict Studies were also relieved of all academic and administrative responsibilities over similar allegations.
Professor Dr Mohammad Bahauddin of the Department of Persian Language and Literature was relieved of his duties over allegations of departmental irregularities and plagiarism in MPhil and PhD theses.
The syndicate formed a committee, led by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Education) Professor Dr Abdus Salam, to review alleged irregularities in the university’s recruitment process between January 2009 and June 2024 and assess the transparency of appointments. The deans of all faculties have been included in the committee.
Another committee, headed by Pro-VC (Administration) Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane, was formed to review research activities conducted under the Higher Education Quality Enhancement Project (HEQEP), funded by the World Bank and the University Grants Commission, during the same period and examine whether project funds were properly utilised.
The Syndicate also decided to take action against individuals, groups and organisations allegedly involved in activities contrary to the spirit of the July mass uprising. It said further decisions will be taken after verification.
In a separate decision, the Syndicate suspended AKM Mahbub Mustafa, supervising engineer (Civil) at the Office of the Chief Engineer, over allegations of activities violating office discipline.
The meeting approved the construction of a July Memorial at the Mall Chattar adjacent to the university's administrative building in memory of those killed during the July mass uprising. The foundation stone of the monument is scheduled to be unveiled on August 5.

item.title: Spider-Man’s loneliest chapter yet
item.description:
This year has been a milestone for Tom Holland.
From getting engaged to longtime partner Zendaya to returning to the role that made him a global star, the British actor seems to be living a life that once existed only in his dreams.
The boy who famously wished to become Spider-Man eventually got to wear the suit.
Now, nearly a decade after his Marvel debut, he is swinging back for another chapter.
Peter Parker, however, has had no such happy ending.
At the close of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the teenager who once had friends, family and mentors was erased from everyone’s memory.
MJ no longer knows him.
Ned Leeds has forgotten their friendship.
Even Doctor Strange’s spell has wiped Peter Parker from the world’s consciousness.
The beloved superhero is left with nothing but his identity as Spider-Man.
That heartbreaking ending sets the stage for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, arriving four years after the events of No Way Home.
The title suggests hope, but for Peter, a “brand new day” means rebuilding his life from absolute zero.
If the film’s trailers and officially revealed details are any indication, that fresh start will be anything but peaceful.
Frank Castle, better known as the Punisher, joins the story as a morally complex ally whose uncompromising brand of justice is likely to clash with Spider-Man’s ideals.
Jon Bernthal reprises the role after his acclaimed appearances in Marvel’s Daredevil series, bringing one of the franchise’s most uncompromising antiheroes into Peter Parker’s world.
The film also welcomes the return of Tombstone, one of New York’s most powerful crime bosses, while Scorpion finally resurfaces after his brief appearance in Spider-Man: Homecoming, promising to settle unfinished business with the web-slinger.
Perhaps the biggest mystery, however, surrounds Bruce Banner.
Promotional footage has teased an enraged Hulk confronting Spider-Man and the Punisher, raising questions about what could push Banner back into losing control.
Meanwhile, Sadie Sink joins the cast in a role Marvel has kept tightly under wraps, fuelling widespread speculation among fans.
Beyond its expanding roster of heroes and villains, Brand New Day reunites the cast that helped define the previous trilogy.
Tom Holland returns as Peter Parker alongside Zendaya as MJ and Jacob Batalon as Ned Leeds.
Their reunion carries particular emotional weight after No Way Home ended with Peter choosing not to reveal himself to the two people who mattered most to him.
The supporting cast also brings together some of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most recognisable faces, including Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner and Jon Bernthal as Frank Castle.
As a result, Brand New Day feels less like a conventional Spider-Man sequel and more like a crossover that could reshape Peter Parker’s place within the wider MCU.
For many viewers, the film also marks the return of a Spider-Man they have grown up with.
Audiences who first met Holland’s Peter Parker in Captain America: Civil War in 2016 have watched the character evolve from an eager teenager desperate to impress Iron Man into a hero defined by sacrifice and loss.
Along the way, Peter has lost his mentor Tony Stark, his Aunt May, his closest friends and, ultimately, his place in the world.
That emotional journey may prove to be Brand New Day’s greatest strength.
For the first time in Holland’s Spider-Man saga, Peter has no safety net. No mentor. No Avengers to rely on. No friends waiting at the end of the battle.
He has to discover who Spider-Man is when no one remembers Peter Parker.
Filmed across New York City, Glasgow and Basingstoke, the movie also returns the character to the city that has always been central to his identity.
Yet its biggest question is not where Peter will go next or which villain he will face.
It is who he will become.
Tom Holland once dreamed of becoming Spider-Man.
Now he returns to portray a Peter Parker who has lost almost everything except the mask.
Perhaps that is what Brand New Day truly means.
After losing everything that once defined him, Peter must decide what kind of hero remains when there is no one left to remember the boy behind the mask.

item.title: Experts: Institutionalizing early disability identification can transform lives
item.description:
Early identification and intervention for children with disabilities should be institutionalized to improve lifelong outcomes and reduce social and economic costs, experts said at a June 24 roundtable organized by the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD) with Liliane Fonds.
Findings from a 2024–2026 project in Barguna and Chattogram showed early screening boosted access to healthcare, rehabilitation, education and social protection, while strengthening caregiver confidence. But limited specialist services, weak referrals, stigma and financial hardship still hinder timely support.
Speakers urged stronger coordination among government, NGOs and partners, expansion of therapy and inclusive education, better referral pathways, digital screening, improved data management and a larger skilled workforce. They emphasized accessible, family‑centred services, greater public awareness and sustained investment in community‑based rehabilitation.
The policy brief recommended integrating disability screening into primary healthcare, strengthening referrals, expanding rehabilitation, supporting caregivers, promoting inclusive education and ensuring sustainable financing.
“Early identification and intervention are critical to ensuring that children and youth with disabilities reach their full potential. While Bangladesh has made significant progress in reducing child mortality, greater attention is needed to developmental support during the first 1,000 days of a child’s life and beyond. Strengthening referral pathways, expanding access to health, education and social services, and supporting families with timely information and care can make a lasting difference. Children in climate-vulnerable and geographically isolated areas deserve equal opportunities, and coordinated action across government, communities and service providers is essential to ensure inclusive development for all.”
“Investing in early identification and intervention for children with developmental delays and disabilities is not only a social responsibility but also an economic necessity. Evidence shows that timely intervention significantly improves children’s development and reduces long-term costs for families and the state. Many children in rural and underserved areas still lack access to screening and support services, while misconceptions often delay treatment and care. Strengthening referral systems, expanding access to services, and raising awareness among families are crucial. The experiences gathered from communities highlight the need for coordinated action so that every child can reach their full potential and contribute meaningfully to society.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical to improving outcomes for children with disabilities, particularly in underserved communities. Through this project, we identified around 1,500 children in two vulnerable upazilas and connected them with screening, rehabilitation, referral, nutrition and assistive device supports. We also worked with caregivers, teachers and local communities to reduce stigma and strengthen inclusive education. Our experience shows that coordinated action across health, education and social protection sectors can significantly improve access to services and ensure that children with disabilities receive the support they need to develop, learn and participate fully in society.”
“Early identification and intervention for children with disabilities and developmental delays reduces long-term public costs. A recent project end learning assessment in the coastal sub-districts of Banshkhali, Chattogram, and Patharghata, Barguna, proves that community-led initiatives, including caregiver involvement, home visits by community interns, and stronger referral lines, greatly improve access to vital services in these remote areas. Despite this progress, social stigma and a lack of specialist care remain significant barriers. Moving forward, the key to leaving no child behind lies in embedding early identification directly into public systems and strengthening community-based support.”
“When my daughter was five, she could neither walk properly, feed herself, nor respond when called. We had consulted many doctors but saw little improvement. Through community outreach support under the EIEI project, we received guidance, home-based exercises, nutritional support, and referrals. Gradually, she began walking, eating on her own, and interacting with others. Most importantly, she is now attending school alongside other children. This support transformed not only my daughter’s life but also our family’s future. Every child with a disability deserves the same opportunity, care, and chance to reach their potential.”
“As a woman with a physical disability, working as a community intern in a remote coastal area was never easy. Yet over 18 months, I witnessed remarkable transformations children once confined to beds began walking, speaking, and attending school. The greatest barrier was not disability itself, but stigma and lack of awareness. When families received support, guidance, and hope, they embraced inclusion. My experience proves that with timely intervention and community support, every child can thrive, and no disability should stand in the way of dignity, education, or opportunity.”
“Our field experience clearly shows that many disabilities could be prevented or mitigated through early identification and timely intervention. Families travel long distances seeking support because specialized rehabilitation services remain scarce at the community level. What stood out most was the overwhelming demand for care and the transformative impact of awareness, screening, and referral services. Disability should not remain a peripheral issue in development planning. Greater investment, stronger government support, and scaling up community-based interventions are essential to ensure that children with disabilities receive the care, inclusion, and opportunities they deserve.”
“My own life demonstrates why early identification and intervention matter. A vision impairment caused at age two was not diagnosed until I was six and treated only at 11—after critical developmental years had passed. In contrast, my niece’s eye condition was detected early and successfully managed, preventing lifelong disability. This project shows that timely screening, strong referral pathways, and coordinated action among health, education, and social protection services can significantly reduce functional limitations, improve inclusion, and help children with disabilities reach their full potential.”
“Early identification is the foundation of disability inclusion. If developmental delays and impairments are detected and addressed on time, many children can avoid lifelong disabilities and achieve their full potential. Technology can play a transformative role in accelerating screening and referrals, while disability corners at upazila health complexes can bring services closer to families. However, medical care alone is not enough. Strong collaboration among government agencies, NGOs, social services, and communities is essential to ensure rehabilitation, assistive devices, education, and inclusion. Investing in early intervention today will reduce disability burdens tomorrow.”
“Early identification is not simply about registering children in a database; it is about assessing their needs and ensuring timely intervention. Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in reducing child mortality, but many children who survive still face developmental disabilities and remain underserved. Sustainable progress requires coordinated action among health, social welfare and disability services. Community clinics, health complexes and disability support centres must work as one system. Without strong institutional linkages and continuity of care, gains made through short-term projects risk being lost, leaving vulnerable children behind.”
“Early identification is critical because the first years of a child’s life determine long-term development outcomes. Many children with developmental delays remain undetected due to limited screening tools and weak referral systems at the community level. Bangladesh needs a simple, nationally standardized early screening tool and stronger implementation at union and Upazila levels. Expanding field-level services, increasing trained personnel, updating disability data, and ensuring follow-up on policy recommendations can significantly improve access to support. Early intervention is not only a child rights issue it is an investment in the nation’s future.”
“Early identification and intervention require strong coordination among health, social welfare, education and disability service agencies. While NGOs have demonstrated effective community-based models, scaling them nationwide is the government’s responsibility. Investing in trained community health workers, strengthening doorstep services, engaging caregivers, and expanding local support systems can significantly improve outcomes for children with disabilities. A unified national database linked to birth registration would enable more efficient and inclusive service delivery.”
“Bangladesh has made significant progress in advancing the rights of persons with disabilities, from ensuring participation in BCS examinations to introducing Braille textbooks and enacting the Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act. However, implementation remains the key challenge. Stronger coordination across ministries, reforms in the Rules of Business, and active national committees are essential to ensure inclusive services. Persons with disabilities must be involved in planning and decision-making processes, while education, social protection and support services need greater monitoring and investment so that no one is left behind.”
“Early identification is the first and most important step in ensuring that children with disabilities receive the support they need to reach their full potential. Bangladesh has made significant progress in disability inclusion through laws, institutions and service centres, but challenges remain in expanding quality services and skilled human resources at the grassroots level. The government is working to strengthen rehabilitation and training facilities across the country, while continued collaboration between government agencies, NGOs and development partners will be essential to build a more inclusive society and improve the lives of persons with disabilities.”
“Early identification and intervention are not optional programmes they are a moral obligation. When children with disabilities receive support early, they have a greater chance to develop, participate and thrive. Families also benefit through reduced stress, improved wellbeing and stronger parent-child relationships. Yet too many children are identified too late and too many families continue to face stigma, isolation and a lack of information. Early intervention is not only the right thing to do; it is also one of the smartest investments a country can make. So early identification and early intervention need to be accessible, affordable and family centred. By acting early, we strengthen children, empower families and build a more inclusive and compassionate society.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical not only for children with disabilities but for every child’s development. When challenges are detected early and the right support is provided, children can reach their full potential, families face fewer burdens, and society benefits as a whole. Inclusive education is not merely an education issue it reflects the values of a civilized and developed nation. Strengthening inter-ministerial coordination, improving referral systems, and promoting behavioral change are essential to ensuring that no child is left behind and that every child has an equal opportunity to thrive.”
“Early identification and intervention are essential for helping children with developmental delays and disabilities reach their full potential. Yet many families face barriers due to limited information, delayed diagnosis and inadequate access to specialist services. My own experience as a parent showed how critical timely intervention can be. Bangladesh needs stronger data systems, more trained professionals, better referral pathways and accessible information in Bangla. This is not the responsibility of one institution alone; it requires coordinated action across government, communities and families to ensure that no child is left behind.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical for ensuring that children with disabilities reach their full potential. We need stronger coordination among government agencies, NGOs, health services and educational institutions to build an effective support system. The government is already in a process of expanding disability service centres, mobile therapy services and inclusive education initiatives, but more work remains. Reliable data, trained professionals, caregiver support and greater public awareness are essential to closing existing gaps. We must also strengthen referral pathways and community-based rehabilitation services. This is a long-term commitment that requires collective action, and we remain dedicated to building a more inclusive and accessible future for every child in Bangladesh.”
“Over the past three decades, we have worked to identify the needs of persons with disabilities, test solutions on the ground, and help integrate successful models into government systems. Bangladesh has made notable progress in inclusive education and rehabilitation services, but early identification and intervention must now become a national priority. The earlier a child is identified, the greater the opportunity for development and inclusion.”

item.title: Bangladesh trapped in the cheap clothes tag
item.description:
Bangladesh has retained its position as the world’s second-largest garment exporter, but the global apparel industry’s post-pandemic recovery is exposing a deeper weakness: while competitors move into higher-value products and capture new demand, Bangladesh remains trapped in the image of a low-cost manufacturing hub.
Although global apparel trade expanded by 4.46% to $574.46 billion in 2025-26, Bangladesh’s ready-made garment exports grew by just 0.89%, far behind Vietnam’s 10.53% and Cambodia’s 16.88%, according to industry data.
Manufacturers, economists and exporters say the sluggish performance reflects more than temporary challenges such as gas shortages, high borrowing costs or supply disruptions.
They argue the industry is confronting a structural problem that has become increasingly difficult to overcome: international buyers continue to associate Bangladesh with low-cost, high-volume production and remain reluctant to pay premium prices for complex, high-value garments.
As a result, factories that invest in technical apparel, functional clothing and sophisticated manufacturing often find themselves negotiating against the same low-price expectations attached to basic T-shirts and knitwear.
“International buyers still operate under the assumption that Bangladesh means cheap production,” said Mostafiz Uddin, founder and chief executive of Bangladesh Apparel Exchange.
“They push us for price cuts on complex items while willingly paying higher prices to other sourcing destinations for identical products. Competing solely on price is no longer a viable strategy.”
Industry leaders say the problem is compounded by destructive competition among local manufacturers, many of whom undercut one another to secure orders.
A senior BGMEA official said buyers sometimes offer as little as $5 for heavy winter jackets, prices that barely cover production costs.
“Factories accept orders with little or no profit just to keep production lines running,” the official said.
“That leaves almost nothing to invest in technology, product development or sustainability.”
Economists warn that Bangladesh is also losing competitiveness because it remains heavily dependent on imported synthetic fabrics, chemicals and specialised raw materials, lengthening production lead times at a time when global fashion brands increasingly prioritise speed over labour costs.
“The global apparel market has fundamentally changed,” said Fahmida Khatun, executive director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue.
“Cost is no longer the only deciding factor. Buyers increasingly demand faster delivery, digital traceability, carbon compliance and supply chain transparency. Bangladesh cannot compete effectively without strengthening its backward linkage industries.”
Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at CPD, said blaming weak export growth solely on external conditions ignores longstanding structural weaknesses.
“To shed the ‘cheap labour’ image, Bangladesh must invest aggressively in technical textiles, synthetic fibres, automation and innovation,” he said.
“Remaining dependent on basic cut-and-make production leaves the industry vulnerable to more integrated competitors.”
Analysts say escaping the low-cost trap will require a coordinated shift in industrial policy, including investment in synthetic fibre production, advanced textile manufacturing, automation and green technology, alongside efforts to build long-term partnerships with international brands rather than competing through relentless price cuts.
Without that transition, they warn, Bangladesh risks remaining the world’s second-largest garment exporter by volume while steadily losing ground in the industry’s fastest-growing and most profitable segments.
